ground_truth.description: The rewrite of `_fail_n_pass_n1` replaces the original 'else → return pass' branch (explicitly named 'N+1 (re-merged, no N) → pass') with `raise AssertionError`. The original test deliberately supported the case where N+1 is re-verified alone after N failed and expected it to pass. If the speculative worker re-verifies N+1 after discarding N (the standard discard-and-retry flow), the patched verification function now raises AssertionError instead of returning a passing result, causing the test to error/behave differently rather than exercise the intended path. This is the most likely cause of the unexpected escalation despite review passing.

The `filterwarnings = ["error:..."]` entries are set at the project-wide `[tool.pytest.ini_options]` level, so unawaited-coroutine and sync-test-in-asyncio-class warnings become hard errors for the entire suite, not just merge_queue tests. Any pre-existing test elsewhere that legitimately leaks a coroutine or has a sync test in an `@pytest.mark.asyncio` class will now fail; only the test_steward class split addresses one such case.

The rewritten verify fakes return MagicMock(passed=..., summary=...) instead of the real orchestrator.verify.VerifyResult dataclass. MagicMock invents truthy attributes, so on every mocked failure merge_queue reads verify.timed_out as truthy and bumps _post_merge_verify_timeouts (the loop-breaker path), and verify.failure_report() returns a MagicMock whose repr is interpolated into the blocked reason. Failed-verify tests therefore silently exercise the timeout loop-breaker path; the old AsyncMock fakes had the same flaw, but the change rewrote every one of these construction sites.

The failing-verify fake `AsyncMock(return_value=MagicMock(passed=False, summary='tests failed'))` is written out three times (lines 507, 1332, 2538) next to the existing _mock_verify_pass() helper, with no matching failure helper.

The change converts some verify fakes to MagicMock values but leaves eight others building results as `AsyncMock()` with attributes assigned afterwards (lines ~1059, 2586, 2629, 2666, 2702, 2770, 2825, 2886), which avoid the unawaited-coroutine leak only because they pass or hand-stub failure_report with a lambda. The file now has two idioms for the same fake, and copying the AsyncMock one onto a failure path reintroduces the leak.

Both `_fail_n_pass_n1` verify fakes (test_merge_queue.py:1162 and :2232) take (merge_wt, cfg, module_configs, task_files=None) with no **kwargs, but SpeculativeMergeWorker calls run_scoped_verification with max_retries=0 and is_merge_verify=True. Every call therefore raises TypeError before the body runs and is reported as a 'Verification error' blocked outcome. The change rewrote both bodies (including the new AssertionError guard at 1162), but the rewritten bodies are dead code and the tests exercise the verify-exception path rather than the verify-failed path they describe.

The new filterwarnings comment misdescribes how the filters work. It presents the RuntimeWarning filter and the PytestUnraisableExceptionWarning filter as covering two independent emission paths, but they are coupled: the unawaited-coroutine RuntimeWarning, once turned into an error inside the coroutine finalizer, becomes an unraisable exception that pytest reports as PytestUnraisableExceptionWarning, so a leaking test fails only when both entries are present and removing either one silently disables enforcement. It also says the asyncio mark-mismatch warning is emitted 'at the collection phase', but pytest-asyncio 1.3.0 emits it from pytest_pyfunc_call, i.e. at call time.

The new [tool.pytest.ini_options] block carries about 20 lines of rationale prose (why the regexes anchor on verbs, CPython-version message formats, why no literal colon) that defends the design rather than stating it; it is drift-prone and belongs in the commit message or a doc/test, with a one-line pointer per filter in the config.

Nothing tests that the new filterwarnings entries actually turn an unawaited coroutine or a sync test under an asyncio mark into a failure. They depend on upstream message wording (which the comment itself calls fragile) and only work as a pair, so a pytest/CPython/pytest-asyncio upgrade or an edit could disable them with no signal.

task.title: Fix AsyncMock setup in merge_queue verification tests
task.description:
orchestrator/tests/test_merge_queue.py emits RuntimeWarning 'coroutine AsyncMockMixin._execute_mock_call was never awaited' at merge_queue.py:280 and 987 for several tests (test_verify_failure_returns_blocked, test_speculative_discard_on_failure, test_speculative_events_emitted, test_verifier_remerge_exception_releases_slot, test_speculative_chain_invalidation_propagates, test_speculative_remerge_preserves_duration_ms, test_verify_failure).

Root cause: test sets `mock_verify = AsyncMock()` then `mock_verify.return_value.passed = False`. Accessing `.return_value` on an AsyncMock creates an AsyncMock child and configures it, so when the mock is awaited, an unnecessary coroutine is created and discarded. The suggested fix is `AsyncMock(return_value=SimpleNamespace(passed=False, summary='tests failed'))` or `AsyncMock(return_value=MagicMock(passed=False))`.

Also test_steward.py:1009 test_timeout_counts_dict_initialized_empty is decorated with @pytest.mark.asyncio but is a sync function — fix by removing the asyncio mark from that specific test.

These are test-hygiene issues, not production bugs, but the warnings clutter CI output and mask genuine resource leaks.
